A1.justification: Both PDFs describe DisCoRD, and their shared text, equations, tables and figures are readable. v1 includes Appendices A–E on PDF pages 12–20; v3 ends with references on page 11 despite citing supplementary sections. This material gap limits appendix-specific comparisons and leaves their retention or revision unresolved.

before.justification: v1 reports original motion reconstruction and generation experiments in Tables 1–4, ablations, and user studies in Figure 8 and Appendix C.4.

after.justification: v3 retains original reconstruction, generation and user-study results and reports additional BAMM comparisons and post-refinement experiments in Tables 2 and 5.

M1.justification: The described DisCoRD procedure retains pretrained tokens, repeat–stack–project conditioning, the conditional rectified-flow objective, Euler decoding and windowed training. v3 expands tensor dimensions and explanations without establishing an algorithm or architecture change. The added post-refinement models are experimental controls.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate HumanML3D and KIT-ML text-to-motion, SHOW co-speech gestures, and music-to-dance using AIST++ mixed with HumanML3D. BAMM extends model comparisons within existing coverage. Talking-face and hand-motion generation appear only as future directions in v3.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds BAMM and BAMM with DisCoRD on HumanML3D; BAMM was cited but not evaluated in v1. Table 5 adds feedforward and rectified-flow post-refinement comparators. Existing main-table comparators remain. Retention of v1's additional Appendix D comparator set cannot be checked.

E3.justification: Table 5 replaces reconstruction MPJPE with sJPE and introduces controls that refine MoMask's decoded outputs. Shared dataset preprocessing, principal evaluation metrics and the default 16 sampling steps remain consistent. The PDFs do not establish changed splits or training budgets for retained experiments.

E4.justification: New post-refinement ablations test whether refining decoded motion can match direct token-conditioned decoding. Projection, attention, windowing and sampling-step analyses remain. The human-perception correlation study and four-method trajectory example highlighted in v3 already appear in v1 Appendix C, so these are not new analyses.

E5.justification: v3 removes the reconstruction FID uncertainty values from Table 1 while retaining its point estimates. Table 2 still reports 95% confidence intervals, and Figure 6 retains 20 timing trials. The correlation study's new main-text summary does not establish a new statistical procedure or additional runs.

E6.justification: New HumanML3D rows report BAMM FID of 0.055 and BAMM with DisCoRD of 0.041. Table 5 adds post-refinement results and sJPE scores for ablation variants. Matched main benchmark values and Figure 8 win rates remain unchanged. The reported 2.7-fold correlation advantage summarizes v1's 0.483 versus 0.181 results.

T1.justification: The shared rectified-flow objective and sJPE Equation 5 are unchanged; expanded projection notation explains the existing procedure. However, v1 Appendix C.2 contains explicit Noise/Static sJPE definitions and their decomposition in Equations 6–8. The cited v3 supplementary counterpart is unavailable, preventing a complete comparison of formal content.

C1.justification: Both versions claim framework-compatible continuous decoding of discrete tokens, improved naturalness while preserving faithfulness, and sJPE as an evaluation contribution. Their abstract FIDs remain 0.032 on HumanML3D and 0.169 on KIT-ML. Rewording and additional supporting comparisons do not materially redefine these contributions.

C2.justification: v3 explains T2M-GPT's faithfulness decline through limited tokenizer capacity and one-to-many decoding, and clarifies reconstruction-versus-generation behavior in projection ablations. Section 5 replaces explicit limitations concerning inherited motion-length restrictions and pretrained-model dependence with future directions involving faces, hands and whole-body motion.

D1.justification: v1 Appendix A/Table 6 documents optimizer settings, training budget, window size, architecture and training time; no v3 counterpart is supplied. Observable changes include more explicit projection dimensions and replacing the project-page link with a promise to release code and checkpoints. The broader reproducibility-documentation change remains unresolved.

R1.justification: Related work is substantially revised to cover classical motion generation, diverse conditioning datasets, latent consistency, interaction models and generative priors. New references include MotionLCM, InterMask and residual quantization; several earlier discussions disappear. v3 also explicitly connects sJPE to existing symmetric percentage-error literature, materially expanding its research context.

P1.justification: v3 extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction, related work, method explanations and experimental discussion. It condenses diffusion preliminaries, places condition projection before the decoder explanation, separates user studies from visualizations, and rewrites the conclusion. These are substantial narrative revisions despite a stable core method.

P2.justification: Figure 1 gains trajectory annotations, and Figure 5 becomes a full-width four-method display using material already present in v1 Figure 12. Tables gain colored highlighting and percentage annotations; Table 5 expands and moves. Most central diagrams and plots retain their visual content and the two-column format.

improvement.justification: The added BAMM comparison, post-refinement controls and clearer projection explanation strengthen the paper. However, v3 drops reconstruction uncertainty values and explicit main-text limitations, while its missing referenced supplement prevents assessing retention of v1's implementation recipe, study protocols and auxiliary findings. These competing effects and the material gap prevent a reliable overall quality judgment.
